To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) for many performance criteria, there is an oracle policy that is sufficiently tractable; (2) the oracle policy can be used as an anchor to design a general learning algorithm; and (3) for many of the performance criteria, the learning algorithm is optimal up to a logarithmic factor.

(1) for many natural objectives, the optimal policy is a variant of the UCB policy; (2) for many natural objective functions, the UCB policy is optimal; (3) in the cases where the UCB policy does not perform as well as the oracle policy, the oracle policy is computationally intractable; and (4) the UCB policy, while not necessarily optimal, is computationally tractable.

(1) for any performance metric that satisfies a natural set of conditions, there exists a corresponding oracle policy that is computationally tractable; (2) for a large class of metrics, the oracle policy is computationally tractible; (3) the regret bounds for the oracle policy can be derived in closed form.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental question of what can and cannot be learned in a bandit framework, beyond the standard total reward objective.

the fundamental question: What is the best strategy for a decision maker who has to repeatedly select one among many options, and the goal is not just to maximize the cumulative rewards but rather some more involved performance measure?
a general framework for bandit problems, beyond cumulative objectives.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results provide a general and unifying framework to the design of efficient bandit algorithms for a broad range of non-cumulative objectives.
, for any given objective, if the oracle policy can be implemented in a computationally tractable manner, then a computationally efficient learning algorithm exists for the problem.
the oracle policy can be efficiently constructed for a large class of performance metrics, provided that they are "well-behaved" with respect to the reward distributions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the design of learning policies for bandit problems beyond cumulative objectives is feasible, provided the objective function is not too "path dependent."
the oracle policy is always tractable for cumulative objectives, and that for non-cumulative objectives, tractability depends on the problem structure.

, while in many cases the cumulative criterion is the only sensible objective for the bandit problem, there are many other interesting cases in which the cumulative objective is not the only sensible one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the oracle policy for a given objective is tractable if the objective function satisfies certain monotonicity and concavity conditions with respect to the reward distribution.

the design of learning policies for non-cumulative objectives can be reduced to a tractable optimization over confidence intervals, which can be efficiently implemented using standard optimization techniques.
the standard MAB framework, which has been extensively studied in the past, is in fact a special case of a more general framework that can accommodate a wide range of objectives.
